title: Show HN: Scolast – AI tutor for autodidacts inspired by Bloom's 2 sigma problem
text: I was using Claude to learn physics and I was getting a bit frustrated with the interface (I kept interrupting the conversation to get a quick explainer on something, and there was no good interface for Claude to ask me questions) so I built Scolast! It's an AI tutor that follows Bloom's findings ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom%27s_2_sigma_problem ) that 1 to 1 tutoring, using mastery learning (basically only moving ahead when the student has demonstrated they learned something, but also moving ahead as quickly as possible) can have pretty incredible results, around two standard deviations higher than regular classroom learning. Bloom called it a problem because this was obviously untenable - but it's actually possible now! I also added little side explainers for anything that's confusing, plus worksheets, and I've been iterating on the voice of the tutor, to try to get a sort of Feynman-y focus on the whys and the experiments and experiences that motivated each piece of knowledge. I find that it's quite remarkable, I'm actually retaining some of the physics I've never been able to retain in the past, and it seems useful in a lot of other domains - my wife used it for language learning and to pass a yoga exam; I've used it to learn some machine learning subjects, etc. One interesting side effect is that I find using it quite tiring, and I actually use tokens very slowly compared to agentic coding - when you actually have to read every token carefully you really get your money's worth. Would love to get people's thoughts so I'm throwing in $3 in free tokens while my budget lasts. After that you can buy tokens and I'm charging an extra 10% to cover everything else. Eventually I'd like to hook it up to people's existing subscriptions, I've applied to OAI's program for this, waiting to see if Ant will offer it. Cheers

title: Show HN: I wrote an entire Vim manual over 4 years
text: I'm glad to announce that I'm releasing my new book, Learning to Play Vim. When I started using Vim more than a decade ago, I wished there was a manual out there teaching how to use this fantastic editor step by step, beginning with the foundations up to more advanced features. Of course at the time I did the vimtutor, but it was too dense for me to remember much from it. I also read the entire Vim manual (`:help manual`), but I didn't like it: it was too detailed in places (for example `02.8 Finding help` completely lost me for a while), and other features didn't get the treatment they deserved. So I decided to write my own Vim manual. It took me more than 4 years and 2987 focused pomodoros (1244 hours) of work to finally get it done! The result: - 21 chapters showing the most important Vim features step by step. - 170 exercises with solutions. - Many real-life examples to show how Vim can be used and configured for your own needs. - The related Vim's help pages to dig further into each feature. Most configs are both written in Vimscript and Lua for Neovim users. This book explores the common features between Vim and Neovim, so don't expect anything about Neovim-specific features (like treesitter or LSP for example). - The landing page: https://themouseless.dev/vim/ - A sample of the book with the entire table of contents and the first three chapters covering most of the basics: https://themouseless.dev/content/learning_to_play_vim_sample... . I wrote this with my bare hands, no LLM involved to spoil the fun.
